title: Biomedical Open Case Studies: Assessing Quality, Normalization, and Expression Patterns in Spatially-Informed Gene Expression Data
text:
Summary


In summary, Xenium technology utilizes a panel of gene-specific probes to assay the spatially-resolved expression for a targeted set of genes at a single-cell or sub-cellular resolution within tissue samples. Samples for Xenium analysis are prepared from either fresh frozen (FF) or formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue blocks. While preparation protocols differ by sample type (e.g, FF or FFPE), generally tissue sections are taken from the tissue block, mounted on specialized slides, and undergo chemical treatments for fixation, permeabilization, probe hybridization, and staining. Following sample preparation, imaging cycles are performed using a Xenium Analyzer. The Xenium Analyzer’s onboard software performs nuclear and cellular segmentation to approximate boundaries between cells and assign observed transcripts to individual cells. Xenium platforms use automated real-time quality control to remove noise and lower quality data. Researchers receive a variety of data including data that reports on the localization of cells, nuclei, and transcripts, observed counts for the transcripts, and morphology images for the tissue sample sections.

title: Biomedical Open Case Studies: Assessing Quality, Normalization, and Expression Patterns in Spatially-Informed Gene Expression Data
text:
Data context

The data used in this case study are from Kwon et al. (2026) which collected dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) samples postmortem from neurotypical donors and donors with diagnosed schizophrenia. Samples were fresh frozen following collection prior to spatial transcriptomics dataset generation. Kwon et al. (2026) generated data using both the Visium and Xenium platforms, using analysis of the Visium data to inform what Xenium data to collect. Visium data was generated for all donors as explained in Supplementary Table 1 while Xenium data was generated for a subset of these donors. For donors where both Visium and Xenium datasets were generated, the tissue samples originated from the same fresh frozen tissue block or source for each donor, but the samples themselves (used to generate the data for each platform) are from adjacent tissue sections of each block. Since each platform requires its own slide mounting and chemical reagents, typically serial tissue sectioning is used to yield adjacent / comparable tissue samples that can be used for multiple experiments with different technologies.
Postmortem tissue samples from 24 donors were used to generate Xenium data. Twelve of those donors had been diagnosed with schizophrenia (denoted by SCZ within the study and this case study) while the other 12 were neurotypical (denoted by NTC within the study and CTRL within this case study).

This case study will work solely with the Xenium data, using only 6 of the 24 samples (3 CTRL and 3 SCZ).

We will work with a reduced number of samples in order to keep the size of the data more manageable. It’s important, especially in studies involving visualization of tissue sections, to work with multiple tissue sections per case (e.g., CTRL vs SCZ) to make sure that signal is not an artifact of how that sample was processed or cut and instead is generalizable across tissue sections/samples.


Matching sample demographics

Typically studies match donor demographics between case cohorts (e.g., having comparable average ages or number of individuals of each sex). Kwon et al. (2026) does this for all of the samples overall as well as the subset of samples that were processed with the Xenium platform, reporting the information in Supplementary Table 1.


The Xenium spatial transcriptomics data represents cellular mRNA counts for panel-targeted genes, mapping the transcripts from those genes to the cellular spatial locations in the tissue (where the probes bound, signifying expression). As such there are 3 main data types or files that we will be working with.

Tissue/sample metadata
Spatial coordinates of cells in the sample
mRNA counts of panel-targeted transcripts for each cell




The panel genes

The panel targets 300 genes using probes designed specifically to target transcripts of these genes:

Six genes (A2M, MAPK3, PLP1, RCAN2, SERPINA3, SOX2-OT) overlap multiple categories within the panel, leading to a total of 300 unique genes represented in the panel. An additional 68 genes already in the panel were also marked as cell type marker genes (beyond the original 35) following further literature review. This can be explored in Supplementary Table 8.

Specific Data Files

Specific data files that we will work with in this case study include files for each of the aspects of the Xenium data:

Sample metadata
Spatial coordinates
mRNA counts


We will be fetching the Xenium generated data (spatial coordinates and mRNA counts) from GEO in the Data Import section of the case study. The project’s GEO accession number for all of the Xenium data is GSE307404. However, each sample has its own specific GEO accession number, which we will use to fetch the data for our reduced number of samples rather than fetching data for all 24 samples.



Previewing available files

We can preview the data files that are available from Xenium for this project using the getGEO() and getGEOSuppFiles() functions from the GEOquery package.

library(GEOquery)


gse <- GEOquery::getGEO("GSE307404", GSEMatrix = TRUE)

Using one sample name from that output, we can what files each sample has.
This let’s us grab a single GEO accession number for a sample from the getGEO results:

pData(gse[[1]])$geo_accession[1]

[1] "GSM9223468"


Then we use that together with the getGEOSuppFiles() function to list the filenames ($fname) deposited for that sample:

GEOquery::getGEOSuppFiles(pData(gse[[1]])$geo_accession[1], fetch_files = FALSE)$fname

The -cells.parquet and -cell_feature_matrix.h5 files are the important files going forward.


Sample metadata
The sample metadata file that we will be working with combines the metadata from Supplementary Table 1 with the GEO accession number for each sample. When using secondary data, it is common for sample metadata to be available in supplementary information. You may need to combine multiple tables of information.


Expansion of metadata from Supplementary Table 1

We previously created a file for the Xenium samples which maps each sample’s GEO Accession Number to the Brain Number ID (geo_to_spatial_samples.csv) and united this with the data from Supplementary Table 1 because we will need the GEO accession number in order to fetch the spatial coordaintes and mRNA counts for each sample. However, the sample metadata file provided in the supplementary table only includes the Brain Number ID (Br####).
The files for this project follow the naming pattern of {sample specific GEO accession number}_{sample Brain Number ID}-{file type specific pattern},

Listed files from GEO accession number GSE307404 (all Xenium data from this project) with list.files() function for one of the file types.
Used stringr::str_replace() function to the specific pattern for that file type with an empty string (""), removing all but the GEO accession number and Brain Number ID (separated by an underscore) for each sample.
Used strsplit("_") function to separate the GEO accession number and Brain Number ID for each string.
Used do.call(rbind.data.frame, .) to create a data frame with the sample GEO accession numbers in the first column and their associated Brain Number IDs in the second column.
Set the column names.
Saved to a .csv file.

Alternatively, we could create this map using the title and geo_accession columns from the pData(gse[[1]]) output we saw earlier.

The combined data from Supplementary Table 1 and the GEO to Brain Number ID map is contained in the file spatial_samples.csv. The spatial_samples.csv file is a file with a header (column names) where values are separated by a comma (.csv). The contents of each column are explained in the following table:



Variable
Details




BrainNumberID
An identifier representing which donor brain the sample originates from. Follows the pattern “Br####”


Race
Demographic information about donors. All samples are “CAUC” for caucasian.


Sex
Demographic information about donors. “M” for male or “F” for female.


Age
Demographic information about donors. Number / decimal representing age of donor in years.


RIN
RNA Integrity Number. Number / decimal representing the quality of the fresh frozen block tissue samples. Generally, Visium and Xenium recommend brain tissues have an observed RIN of 4+ (though older resources may recommend 7+) (Grases and Porta-Pardo (2026)). Lower RINs may lead to reduced sensitivity.


PMI
Postemortem Interval. Number / decimal representing the time interval between the donor’s death and the sample extraction and freezing from that donor. Typically reported in hours, but could be reported in days or another measurement of time. To promote greater fresh frozen block tissue quality, generally it is recommended to minimize the post mortem interval


PrimaryDx
Demographic information about donors representing the primary diagnosis. “Control” for neurotypical donors and “Schizophrenia” for donors diagnosed with schizophrenia.


Visium
“YES” or “NO” for whether Visium data was generated for this sample. All samples are “YES”.


Xenium
“YES” or “NO” for whether Xenium data was generated for this sample.


GEO
The GEO accession number for samples with Xenium data. NA for samples with only Visium data.



The demographic information is useful for data exploration. We will primarily be using the BrainNumberID, PrimaryDx, Xenium, and GEO variables.

The Xenium and GEO variables will be used to select a subset of samples of fetch the data for those samples from GEO.
The BrainNumberID and PrimaryDx variables will be used to create informative sample IDs so that we can more easily observe the case (e.g., CTRL or SCZ) of samples throughout our analysis.



Spatial coordinates
Classically, -cells.parquet files are used to store the spatial coordinates of the cells, specifically the The point corresponding to the geometric center of a shape. Has an x- and y- coordinate associated with it. Can be found if you know the vertices of a polygon.centroid locations (or centers of the cells).
The .parquet file type is a departure from the normal way we would expect data to be stored. Often our file types (e.g., .csv) store data row by row with each row containing a complete record or set of related information about a specific sample, timepoint, etc. Instead, .parquet files store data column-by-column. This leads to more efficient storage and querying of large data files.
Additional information provided in this file is described by 10X genomics.


If -cells.parquet files are not available

Sometimes when you are using publicly available data rather than generating new datasets yourself, files that you may expect are not deposited or archived.
If .parquet files are not available, first check if cells.csv.gz is available as this is an alternate format of the typical file. If not, you can use a different Xenium output to calculate the centroids typically stored in the cells.parquet files. This will be explored further within a click to expand section in the Data Import section of the case study, but this alternate file type is also introduced here:
-cell_boundaries.csv.gz also stores spatial coordinates. Specifically these files have many rows per cell describing each vertex that is part of a polygon, where the polygon edges represent the borders of the cell. We can find the centroid of each cell by considering all of these polygon coordinates together. The contents of this file are the result of the nucleus segmentation algorithm that expands the nuclei DAPI-stained boundaries to determine cell boundaries.







Variable
Details




cell_id
A cell ID corresponding to the barcode variable in the mRNA counts data. Multiple rows will have the same cell_id value in these files.


vertex_x
The x-coordinate of a vertex between two of the edges of the polygon representing that cell.


vertex_y
The corresponding y-coordinate of that vertex between two of the edges of the polygon representing that cell.












Another file output that Xenium provides is nucleus_boundaries. This file is not sufficient for cell spatial coordinates because it’s only providing the boundaries of the nucleus rather than the cells. Nuclear positioning varies across cells, so you can’t make an assumption about the center of cell if you have coordinates for the nucleus.
These file types are described in greater detail by 10X genomics.


This case study will use the arrow package to work with -cells.parquet files for the spatial coordinates data.



mRNA counts
The data for the mRNA counts that we’ll be using is stored in -cell_feature_matrix.h5 files. This file type efficiently stores large amounts of data that are typically represented by large matrices (n rows for genes * m columns for cells with counts for a given gene in a specific cell stored at each intersection). Instead, .h5 files use nested named lists to store the data. Of important note, only non-zero counts are stored as well as the indices where those counts would be located in a matrix (e.g., indices for which genes and cell IDs they would correspond with). These nested named lists can be used to reconstruct the matrix structure of the data.
Note that “features” is an alternative word for genes in this field and will be used interchangeably throughout this case study.
We can use either the rhdf5::h5dump() function or the rhdf5::h5ls() function to get a look at the nested lists (and their names) for this data.
For example:

$matrix is the top list name

$barcodes – nested list under matrix; the cell IDs
$data – nested list under matrix; the non-zero counts
$features – nested list under matrix; has its own nested subparts relating to the rows/genes

$_all_tag_keys – “genome” for our data
$feature_type – specifies “Gene Expression” for the panel genes or Xenium QC probes/codewords such as negative control probe, negative control codeword, or unassigned codeword

$id – gene ID or control/probe ID for elements of $data
$name – gene name or control/probe name for elements of $data

$indices – nested list under matrix; zero-based row index for non-zero values found in $data (i equivalent for Matrix::sparseMatrix() function used in the Data Import section of the case study)
$indptr – nested list under matrix; zero-based index for $data and $indices where columns start (p equivalent of Matrix::sparseMatrix() function in the Data Import section of the case study)
$shape – nested list under matrix; dimensions of the data (number of genes or features X number of cells).

Note that the number of cells >>>>> number of genes (Xenium panel with limited number of genes)
Note that the product of the dimensions will be greater than the length of $data since this data format is representing non-zero counts only and therefore is a sparse representation



The most important parts of this file for us will be barcodes, data, features$name, indices, indptr, and shape. Each of these will be used as we build sparse matrices from the .h5 formatted data.
For more information about the .h5 file format, consider this 10X Genomics resource.


If -cells_feature_matrix.h5 files are not available

Alternative formats for mRNA counts that may be provided as Xenium outputs (MEX or Zarr) are discussed here with specific explanations for Zarr files here. Tools such as Rarr, zarr, XeniumIO, or Seurat may be useful for working with these file types.


This case study will use the rhdf5 and Matrix packages to work with cell_feature_matrix.h5 files for the mRNA counts data.



General note on variety of Xenium outputs
Xenium produces a variety of output files. Not all of these will be shared / deposited into an archive. While some file types may be more usual or preferred by some in the field (e.g., because it’s more efficient to store or it’s a file type they are more comfortable with), there doesn’t appear to be a specific industry standard or accepted practice on files to always use. For example, morphology images (likely stained with DAPI to mark nuclei) are often output but are not always shared. An output may be shared as a .csv file instead of a .parquet file or as a Zarr file instead of an .h5 file. It may seem like you can’t proceed if you don’t see the file types you expect, but it’s not necessarily a lost cause. Make sure that you understand:

What files are available and what they represent about the data. You may be able to use an alternate file type for a specific aspect of the data (e.g., spatial coordiantes).
What file types your downstream tools expect or can work with.
If you can use a file type that you have in place of a file type that you or a downstream tool usually expects, or at least wrangle it to meet your needs.
What (if any) specialized packages are necessary to read in and work with certain file types.



Reproducibility Considerations


If you need a specific file but don’t see it in an archive, contact the study personnel and ask if that file can be added. Data reuse benefits the scientific community and promotes reproducible, robust, and generalizable scientific discovery.

text:
What spatialGE is looking for

spatialGE provides the user flexibility in how they import their data. Users can either provide file paths or they can provide named lists with each list containing data frames for each sample. To better understand the data we have and are working with, we will provide named lists of data frames for both the spatial coordinates and the mRNA/feature counts.
Each named list will use the same sample names to show which data goes with which sample. Each data frame within a given named list will have similar structure, but different underlying data points specific to that sample.










Spatial coordinates
For spatial coordinates, each data frame should have:

3 columns

Cell IDs
X coordinate for the center of the cell
Y coordiante for the center of the cell

One row per each unique cell ID; let’s say we have m cells










We will include a column for the area of each cell for later use in the normalization process, but this is not an expected part of the input by spatialGE.


mRNA counts
For the mRNA counts, each data frame should have:

n rows

1 for each feature
let’s say we have n features.

(m+1) columns

1 for each cell
For our spatial coordinates, we said we had m cells
Add 1 because the first column will list the feature/gene names











Recall that both of these (spatial coordinates and mRNA counts data) will be stored in separate named lists where the names correspond to samples, and each sample has its own data frame.


Sample metadata
spatialGE also requires sample information. We will provide sample names / metadata where the sample names match those used in the named lists. The sample names will be in the first column of the samples metadata data frame (though they could also be passed as just a vector of names).

Subsetting samples
We want to subset 6 samples (3 for each diagnosis) from the larger set of samples so that we still have multiple samples to compare, but aren’t working with every possible sample as that would require a lot of memory and storage (as explained in the What are the data? section of the case study).

set.seed(567)
spatial_sample_info <- readr::read_csv(here::here("data/raw/spatial_samples.csv"))
spatial_sample_info <- spatial_sample_info %>%
  dplyr::filter(Xenium == "YES")

#3 NTC samples
ntc_samples <- unname(sample(unlist(spatial_sample_info[which(spatial_sample_info$PrimaryDx == "Control"), "GEO"]), 3))

#3 SCZ samples
scz_samples <- unname(sample(unlist(spatial_sample_info[which(spatial_sample_info$PrimaryDx == "Schizophrenia"), "GEO"]), 3))

samples <- c(scz_samples, ntc_samples)

samples

[1] "GSM9223484" "GSM9223483" "GSM9223479" "GSM9223485" "GSM9223477"
[6] "GSM9223481"





What is this code doing?


We set the random seed.
We read in the sample metadata file.
We filter the data frame to include only samples used for Xenium data generation.
We subselect 3 random CTRL samples from all samples where the primary diagnosis is “Control” (PrimaryDx == "Control") using the sample() function.
We subselect 3 random SCZ samples from all samples where the primary diagnosis is instead “Schizophrenia”, again using the sample() function.
We make a vector combining those 6 sample IDs.





Reproducibility considerations


Any steps in an analysis that rely on randomness or stochasticity are not reproducible later or by others unless a random seed is set prior to the running those steps (and that specific random seed is then used every time before running those steps).

section: Fetching GEO data for these samples
text:
Fetching GEO data for these samples

This lapply will loop through the samples vector and fetch the following files for each sample from GEO using the getGEOSuppFiles() function from the GEOquery package:

-cell_boundaries.csv.gz for computing spatial coordinates (a side quest explored later in a click to expand section)
cells.parquet.gz for spatial coordinates
-cell_feature_matrix.h5 for mRNA counts




How does lapply or “loop”ing work?

A function like the getGEOSuppFiles() function from the GEOquery package accepts inputs and performs specified steps with that input, providing some output following those steps.
When you use a loop to call a function for a set of inputs, the loop provides each input individually to the function. For each individual input, the function performs its specified steps and produces an output. Then the loop gives the function the next input and the process is repeated until there are no more inputs to give the function.









We’ll use an example with lab pets to show this in a more concrete way.









We could specify a loop (that doesn’t use or call a function yet), but just goes through each of the lab members who has a cat and outputs their cat’s name. Outside of the loop, we could specify the dog’s name for the fourth lab member who has a dog, not a cat. Because that last part is happening outside of the loop, it is only output once rather than being output every time we go through the loop. And the number of times we go through the loop relates to the number of inputs we’re looping through (in this case 3 because there are 3 lab members with cats).









We could write a function that generalizes that process, specifically reporting the lab member and who their pet is, even specifying whether that pet is a dog or a cat, after evaluating the input. Functions are especially useful in cases like this where there is a process that has related tasks with specifiable, but slightly different behavior dependent on how an input is evaluated.


















Notice that we have to explicitly call this function for every lab member that we want to use it for. We would have to call the function four times, one for each lab member. Generally, we want to reduce redundancy in our code, so it might make sense to use a loop to loop through our data and call the function multiple times that way.
To reduce redundancy, we could call the function with a for loop. Notice because of how we defined our function, the lab member with a dog is part of the for loop now, instead of outside of it!









lapply is another function that provides the functionality of a loop, meant specifically to work with functions. One intricacy of lapply is that the output from calling the function for a set of a items is returned in a list. (That’s what the l in lapply stands for: “list”.) Given that we’ve said that we want our spatialGE inputs to be in named lists, lapply will be helpful for us in constructing those inputs down the line.












How to construct an lapply statement

lapply statements have 2 parts.

Some iterable object such as a list or vector. This may be:


a named list
a vector with character elements
a vector of indices (1:length(some_vector)).


Some function to apply for each element of the iterable object. This may be:


a base R function
a function from a loaded package or library
a function you’ve defined elsewhere in your code

If you iterate directly over a named list, the output list from lapply will use the same names from the input for the corresponding output. If you instead iterate using a vector of indices, the list won’t have names and you may need to name the output yourself.
For more explanation and examples of using lapply, consider the post Andrews (2021) or the function’s documentation.


A regex pattern is used to specify which files to download (there are more available than just these 3 for each sample).


Details on the regex pattern

Regex is another term for a regular expression that is used to match a pattern. In this case, we’re matching any one of 3 patterns and asking GEOquery to fetch only the files that match one of these 3 patterns.

The “or” like behavior of this is from the vertical pipes (| ) in the regex.
The double backslashes (\\) are escape characters which are used in front of special or meta characters (e.g., ., *, -, +) that may otherwise be used for specific, programmatic purposes aside from literal string matching. Using an escape character in front of the special character is necessary to make sure they are considered as literal characters within the string matching rather than any special purpose or role they may serve. If only a single backslash was used, R would evaluate and drop that backslash, passing only the “unescaped” special character to regex. Therefore we have to also escape the backslash that regex uses. R will recognize and drop the first one in its string parsing, while the second backslash will remain and be recognized by the regex parsing, escaping the special characters (a dash or period in this case).



lapply(1:length(samples), 
       function(x) 
       GEOquery::getGEOSuppFiles(GEO = samples[x], 
                      filter_regex = "\\-cell_boundaries|\\-cell_feature_matrix|\\.parquet", 
                      baseDir = here("data/raw")
                      )
      )

Note: You will need about 127 M (Megabytes) or (0.127 GB / Gigabytes) available on your system to fetch and store this data using this code.
Typically, lapply returns outputs from calling the specified function in a list. Because we don’t need to store anything in R from this function (getGEOSuppFiles is going to store files in our computer’s file system where we tell it to instead.), we’re not going to assign the output to any variables. We could use a for loop here instead of lapply and it would work just as well. However, lapply is a tad more efficient at looping in R than for loops, so we use it here for its efficiency gains rather than how it outputs the function outputs.

text:
Preparing the data for import into spatialGE (with STlist)

Now that we’ve fetched our data from GEO, we can work with it to make sure that we understand what it contains and that it’s in the correct formats that spatialGE expects.

Sample metadata
We will use the samples vector that we created earlier to subset our spatial sample metadata to include only those 6 samples, and we will create a new column that can serve as a more informative sample ID (reporting not just a sample ID but also the primary diagnosis / case) for our use throughout this case study.

lookup <- c(sampleID = "GEO", brainNumID = "BrainNumberID")
samples_metadata <- spatial_sample_info %>% 
  dplyr::rename(., all_of(lookup)) %>%
  dplyr::filter(sampleID %in% samples) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(PrimaryDx = case_when(PrimaryDx == "Control" ~ "CTRL", 
                               PrimaryDx == "Schizophrenia" ~ "SCZ")
        ) %>% 
  tidyr::unite("DxID", 
               brainNumID, PrimaryDx, 
               sep = "", 
               remove = FALSE) %>%
  dplyr::relocate(DxID) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(match(sampleID, samples))

samples_metadata

  DxID       brainNumID Race  Sex     Age   RIN   PMI PrimaryDx Visium Xenium

1 Br5973SCZ  Br5973     CAUC  F      61.4   8.5  22   SCZ       YES    YES   
2 Br1139SCZ  Br1139     CAUC  F      44.9   8.7  44   SCZ       YES    YES

# ℹ 1 more variable: sampleID <chr>





What is this code doing?


Rename some column names.
Filter the data frame to include only the subset samples from the samples vector.
Combine the Brain Number ID with the Primary Dx to create a sample ID that provides more information about each sample.
Relocate this new ID to be the first column (because this is the sample ID we want spatialGE to use when we input our data).
Arrange so the rows are in the same order as the samples vector.



Let’s get rid of the other data frames and extra vectors so we don’t accidentally use them going forward and to reclaim some memory.

rm(spatial_sample_info, ntc_samples, scz_samples, samples, lookup)



Spatial Coordinates

Files from Kwon et al. (2026) use the following naming convention:
{sample specific GEO accession number}_{sample Brain Number ID}-{file type specific pattern}


Reproducibility considerations


Using consistent file naming schemes within a project is an important reproducibility consideration. One reason is because this practice supports more automated data retrieval and handling, reducing the risk of errors from manual processes. For more, consider the ITCR’s Introduction to Reproducibility in Cancer Informatics course’s discussion on the topic or this File naming and organization guide from UT Dallas


We will utilize the consistent naming conventions as we construct file paths in order to read in the files to work with them, specifically iterating over the samples to construct the file paths.

For each sample, we want to read in the relevant file, process it (storing the data spatialGE needs in a dataframe) and then storing each sample’s data frame in a named list. Using lapply again will be a good fit for this.
Because we’re working with the spatial coordinates data, our file type specific pattern will be -cells.parquet.gz. Notice that these files are compressed (denoted by the .gz file extension) and the arrow package (which is typically used to read and wrangle .parquet files), needs them to not be compressed in order to read them in.

decompress_read_parquet <- function(samples_metadata, sample){
  #Build file paths
  gz_file <- here(paste0("data/raw/",
                         sample,
                         "/",
                         sample,
                         "_",
                         samples_metadata[which(samples_metadata$sampleID == sample), "brainNumID"],
                         "-cells.parquet.gz"))
  
  decompressed_file <- str_replace(gz_file, ".gz", "")

  #Decompress
  R.utils::gunzip(gz_file, destname = decompressed_file, remove = FALSE, skip = TRUE)

  #Read in
  df <- arrow::read_parquet(decompressed_file)

  #Remove the decompressed file because we no longer need it
  file.remove(decompressed_file)
  
  #Select columns of interest
  centroids <- df %>%
    dplyr::select(cell_id, x_centroid, y_centroid, cell_area)

  #reclaim some R resources
  rm(df, gz_file, decompressed_file)
  gc()

  #Return
  return(centroids)

}

spatial_coords <- lapply(1:nrow(samples_metadata), function(x) decompress_read_parquet(samples_metadata, samples_metadata$sampleID[x]))
names(spatial_coords) <- samples_metadata$DxID




What is this code doing?


We define a function that we can call with lapply in order to process the parquet files and produce a list to give to spatialGE eventually.
We construct the path for a given sample’s cell centroid coordinates .parquet file, using our sample metadata data frame to match the GEO sample ID we’re giving the function to the corresponding sample brain number ID also needed for the file path.
We create a string for what a decompressed version of the file should be named.
We decompress the file, storing it in our file system
We read in the data with the arrow package and its read_parquet() function.
We remove the decompressed file from our file system because we no longer need it.
We select only the columns that spatialGE needs, reporting the centroid coordiantes for each cell and a column we can use for normalization later:


cell_id
x_centroid
y_centroid
cell_area (for later normalization)


We remove some variables that are no longer needed to reclaim some R resources.
We return a data frame with only those 3 columns.





What if you don’t have the canonical parquet files?


testsample <- samples_metadata$sampleID[1]

df_test_sample <- read_csv(here(paste0("data/raw/",
                                 testsample,
                                 "/",
                                 testsample,
                                 "_",
                                 samples_metadata[which(samples_metadata$sampleID == testsample), "brainNumID"],
                               "-cell_boundaries.csv.gz")))

centroids <- df_test_sample %>%
    dplyr::group_by(cell_id) %>%
    dplyr::slice(1:n(), 1) %>%
    dplyr::summarize(geometry = sf::st_sfc(st_polygon(list(cbind(vertex_x, vertex_y)))), .groups = "drop") %>%
    sf::st_as_sf() %>%
    mutate(centroid = sf::st_centroid(geometry)) %>% #compute centroid location for each cell
    mutate(cx = sf::st_coordinates(centroid)[,1],
           cy = st_coordinates(centroid)[,2]) %>%
    sf::st_drop_geometry() %>% #so that we can grab just the cell IDs and centroid x,y values
    select(cell_id, cx, cy)

This method

Uses a similar method to read in the data files as the decompress_read_parquet() function we defined, but it


doesn’t need to decompress them first because read_csv from readr can handle compressed files.
uses -cell_boundaries.csv.gz as the file type specific pattern.


We group the data by the cell_id column since multiple rows are present for each cell ID.
(with slice) We have to append the first row for each cell ID also to the bottom in order to “close the polygon” by going back to the starting vertex.
We grab coordinates for each cell’s polygon vertices and store all coordinates in a geometry column.
(with st_as_sf()) We convert the data frame into a simple feature object so that we can work within a spatial context (to compute the cell’s centroid) for non-spatial data structures.
(with st_centroid()) We compute the centroid location for each cell using the geometry column created earlier.
We grab the x and y coordinates for the centroids, storing them in their own columns within the feature object.
(with st_drop_geometry()) We drop the geometry or feature object aspect of the data so that we’ll be able to select just the columns we want in a dataframe.
We store the Cell IDs and centroid coordinates as a dataframe for that sample.

This method is accurate if compared to the parquet files.

dplyr::right_join(spatial_coords[[unlist(samples_metadata[which(samples_metadata$sampleID == testsample), "DxID"])]],
           centroids,
           by = "cell_id") %>%
    rename(x_dataset_parquet = x_centroid, 
           y_dataset_parquet = y_centroid, 
           x_dataset_compute = cx, 
           y_dataset_compute = cy) %>% 
    tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = - cell_id, 
                 names_to = c("variable", "dataset"), 
                 names_pattern = "(x|y)_(.*)") %>% 
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = dataset, 
                values_from = value) %>% 
    ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = dataset_parquet, 
               y = dataset_compute)) + 
      ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.2) + 
      ggplot2::facet_wrap(~variable) + 
      ggpubr::stat_regline_equation(aes(label =  paste(..eq.label.., ..rr.label.., sep = "*`,`~")),

(`stat_regline_equation()`).

(`geom_point()`).










Join the earlier results from the test sample that we stored in the named list with the results from this computation approach (centroids) so that we have 5 columns of data (the cell_id and the x and y coordinates from each method)
Rename the columns so they are more informative
Pivot the data longer for every column except the cell_id column such that there will be 4 columns (the cell_id, a column with each coordinate value (named value), and two columns describing where each coordinate value is from: (variable x or y) and dataset (computed or parquet)).
We then use pivot wider to create two columns from the single dataset column so that the parquet coordinate values are in their own column and the computed coordinate values are in their own column. This final dataframe has 4 columns


cell_id
variable: x or y
dataset_parquet: the x or y coordinate for that cell_id from the parquet file
dataset_compute: the x or y coordinate for that cell_id from the computation method


This is passed to ggplot where we create scatter plots of the dataset_parquet coordinates on the x-axis and the dataset_compute coordinates on the y-axis for two different panels (facet_wrap) with one panel comparing the x coordinates and one panel comparing the y coordinates.
We add a regression line with a label for the regression coefficient and R^2 value.




mRNA counts
Earlier we explored what the .h5 files look like because reading in the mRNA counts from the h5 files requires that we know the names used in those files.

read_rna <- function(samples_metadata, sample){

  h5file <- here(paste0("data/raw/",
                         sample,
                         "/",
                         sample,
                         "_",
                         samples_metadata[which(samples_metadata$sampleID == sample), "brainNumID"],
                        "-cell_feature_matrix.h5"))
                              

  rna_h5data <- rhdf5::h5read(h5file, name = "matrix")

  rna_mat <- Matrix::sparseMatrix(i = rna_h5data$indices,
                       p = rna_h5data$indptr,
                       x = as.integer(rna_h5data$data),
                       dims = rna_h5data$shape,
                       index1 = FALSE) %>%
      as.matrix() %>%
      as.data.frame() %>%
      `rownames<-`(rna_h5data$features$name) %>%
      `colnames<-`(rna_h5data$barcodes) %>%
      tibble::rownames_to_column("genes")

  rm(rna_h5data, h5file)
  gc()

  return(rna_mat)
}

rnacounts_input <- lapply(1:nrow(samples_metadata), function(x) read_rna(samples_metadata, samples_metadata$sampleID[x]))
names(rnacounts_input) <- samples_metadata$DxID




What is this code doing?


We define a function that we can call with lapply in order to process the .h5 files and produce a list to give to spatialGE eventually.
Uses a similar method to read in the data files as our previous decompress_read_parquet() function for the parquet files, but it


doesn’t need to decompress them

uses -cell_feature_matrix.h5 as the file type specific pattern.


We read in the corresponding cell feature matrix file using h5read() from the rhdf5 package. This package requires a name parameter which corresponds to the name of the top list. In the What are the data? section of the case study, we found that name to be “matrix”.
We build a sparse matrix, using the elements of the .h5 file that correspond to each argument


i: specifies the positions or indices of the rows with non-zero values in the matrix – indices from the .h5 file.
p: specifies the first column with a non-zero value for each row – indptr from the .h5 file.
x: non-zero values for the matrix entires – data from the .h5 file.
dims: matrix dimensions – shape from the .h5 file.
index1 we set to FALSE because our values are 0-based indices meaning that we start counting indices from 0 instead of 1.


We expand the sparse matrix to be a dense matrix that can then be turned into a data frame.
We set the row names to be the feature names from the .h5 file (features$name)
We set the column names to be the cell IDs from the .h5 file (barcodes)
We also move the rownames to the first column and name it “genes” because spatialGE looks for gene names in the first column, not as rownames, making sure they are unique..
Finally we store this data frame in our named list for that sample

text:
Preparing a spatialGE object with STlist

We can import our data in a way that the spatialGE package can work with it, by using the STlist() function from spatialGE. This function creates an object in a standardized format that spatialGE functions can utilize in a predictable and generalizable way across datasets.

scz_spatial <- spatialGE::STlist(rnacounts = rnacounts_input,
                                 spotcoords = spatial_coords,
                                 samples = samples_metadata
                                )

Found list of dataframes.
Matching gene expression and coordinate data...
Converting counts to sparse matrices
Completed STlist!





Alternative way to import the data using only file paths

If we tried to read in the data directly following fetching it from GEO, we would get a warning message about not being able to find the coordinates for each sample.
So first, we would have to decompress the cells.parquet.gz files for each sample. Once we’ve done that, we would be able to use the following code to read in the data with spatialGE doing all of the work to extract the data from the Xenium outputs. This code lists the directories where the files are located so that spatialGE can look in those directories for the files it expects. You only have to provide these file paths to the rnacounts paramter. You also have to provide it with the samples it should be looking for. These are the names of the directories.

rnacounts <- paste0(here("data/raw/"), list.files(here("data/raw/"), pattern = "GSM"))

#rnacounts would be a list of the directories, but not the files themselves.

scz_spatial <- STlist(rnacounts = rnacounts, samples = str_replace(rnacounts, here("data/raw/"), ""))

One downside of this approach is that it’s using the GEO accession numbers as the sample ID that spatialGE is going to use going forward. We would have to change the directory names to have different sample names.


We will explore this object (what it contains, how to access it, etc.) in the Data Exploration section of the case study.
First, let’s release some memory for variables we don’t need anymore.

rm(spatial_coords, rnacounts_input, centroids, df_test_sample, testsample)

Because we have had to do some work in order to import the data, we will save the spatialGE object to an .rds file that can be used later without needing to repeat these steps.

text:
The STlist object

We can look at the type of an object using the typeof() function.

typeof(scz_spatial)

[1] "S4"


The STlist object is an S4 class in R. This means that the object has “slots”. Slots are accessed using an @, rather than a $ (which you would use for a list or data frame column).
Typically you would see the names in a list using the names() function. Instead, for an S4 class object you use the function slotNames().

slotNames(scz_spatial)

[1] "counts"       "spatial_meta" "gene_meta"    "sample_meta"  "tr_counts"   
[6] "gene_krige"   "misc"        


With an S4 class, you have to pre-specify slots prior to the object’s creation. You can’t add slots as you go through an analysis. Therefore, some of these slots currently have data and others will have data added once some spatialGE functions are used. In this case, the S4 object spatialGE uses has its slots pre-specified by the package developers. We, the package users, will not be able to create any new slots.
If we tried to assign a new slot, we would see an error.

scz_spatial@test <- "This is a test"


Error in (function (cl, name, valueClass) : ‘test’ is not a slot in class “STlist”


Slots with data currently
Several of the slots have data already just from us loading the data with spatialGE.

counts
The counts slot stores a named list

typeof(scz_spatial@counts)

[1] "list"


The named list stores sparse matrices of gene counts – one sparse matrix for each sample.

names(scz_spatial@counts)

[1] "Br1139SCZ"  "Br5314CTRL" "Br5746SCZ"  "Br5973SCZ"  "Br8433CTRL"
[6] "Br8667CTRL"

spatial_meta
Similarly, the spatial_meta slot stores a named list.

typeof(scz_spatial@spatial_meta)

The named list stores tibbles (a type of data frame) of metadata for cells in each sample. text:
Filtering


Using Control Probes and Codewords
First we create a function that we can use with lapply that takes the filtering thresholds that we found previously as well as each counts matrix as inputs. Notice that the thresholds are named arguments meaning they have default values set to the exact variables we were working with earlier. We don’t have to specify them when we call the function because they have these default values. We find the combined expression within each cell of each of the three associated controls using column sums and identify the cell IDs where the combined expression of any one of these types of controls is greater than or equal to the 99th percentile threshold. Finally, we take a union of the identified cell IDs.
By calling this function with lapply, we’ll have a named list (to_remove_all) where each sample name stores a vector of cell IDs that should be removed for that sample.
We use a for loop to then loop through the sample names and actually filter the cell IDs within the count matrix. Recall that the cells correspond to the columns in the count matrix. Our filter is specifically using an exclamation point (!) to specify that if a column name is not the list of cell IDs to be filtered, then keep it.
We use a for loop for the actual filtering because we don’t want to output a list. Rather we want to overwite the counts slot, doing the same filtering steps for all of the samples (just using a different set of cell IDs to keep).

findOverlap <- function(mat, negcp = negcontrol_probe_cutoff, negcc = negcontrol_cdwd_cutoff, ucc = unassigned_cdwd_cutoff){
    which_negcp <- names(which(mat[startsWith(rownames(mat), "NegControlProbe"), ] %>% Matrix::colSums() >= negcp))
    which_negcc <- names(which(mat[startsWith(rownames(mat), "NegControlCodeword"), ] %>% Matrix::colSums() >= negcc))
    which_ucc <- names(which(mat[startsWith(rownames(mat), "Unassigned"), ] %>% Matrix::colSums() >= ucc))

    to_remove <- union(union(which_negcp, which_negcc), which_ucc)

    return(to_remove)
}

text:
Normalizing
Transforming the raw mRNA counts is again necessary because of technical biases. Typically if working with single cell RNAseq data or data from sequencing based spatial transcriptomics assays (e.g., Visium), normalization methods try to correct for different sequencing depths in different cells. Typical methods used include log-transformation or the SCTransform method. The spatialGE package allows users to implement either of these with their spatially-resolved gene expression data. However, both of these methods are best suited to working with sequencing-based data rather than image-based data. Atta et al. (2024) and Bhuva et al. (2024) discuss how these traditional methods may not be appropriate for spatial transcriptomics data, especialy data from image-based technologies. Atta et al. (2024) recommends using cell volume or cell area when available to normalize image-based data. Bhuva et al. (2024) introduces a method SpaNorm which models library size effects while taking into account the spatial information inherent in the data. The SpaNorm method can’t directly work with an STlist object from spatialGE without first converting it to a SpatialExperiment or Seurat object. Therefore, we won’t perform normalization with SpaNorm within this case study. We will perform normalization with the typical methods and a cell area normalization.
Transformed counts are stored in the tr_counts slot and we can’t store more than one set of transformed counts due to the “slot” nature of the data. Since we want to run more than one method and compare them, we will need multiple different spatialGE STlist objects. We’ll duplicate two here, one that we can use with SCTransform and one we can use with a cell area normalization.

scz_spatial_tr <- rlang::duplicate(scz_spatial)
scz_spatial_sct <- rlang::duplicate(scz_spatial)


Log Transformation
Explain log transformation.

scz_spatial <- spatialGE::transform_data(scz_spatial, method='log', cores=2)

When spatialGE performs normalization, besides adding data to the tr_counts slot for the transformed data, it also does a couple of other tasks. First, it fills in the gene_meta slot. Previously this had been an empty list. Now it stores a data frame for each sample with the average and standard deviation expression for each gene.

Cell Area Normalization
Atta et al. (2024) recommends using cell volumes to normalize image-based data when it is available, but that cell area can be used instead. We do not have cell volumes, but we do have cell areas.

We recommend, as first choice, cell volume normalization to account for such partial cell capture within imaged regions. Cell area may serve as a proxy where volume estimates are not available.

The spatialGE package does not currently support any additional normalization methods besides log-transformation and SCTransform. However, we can perform an alternate normalization method and store its results in our STlist object (scz_spatial), using data already present in scz_spatial because we brought over the cell_area column for each cell earlier in the Data Import section of the case study.
The cell area normalization procedure requires that:

We find the median cell area for each sample
Then find cell specific size factors by dividing each cell’s area by the median.
We then scale the counts by these size factors.
Finally, similarly to the log transformation method, we add a pseudocount of one so that there are no zeros before we use a logarithm to bring the values closer together.

This approach is used in the OSTA book chapter for Xenium workflows and adapts code from the scrapper package.
Beyond performing and storing our cell area normalization, we’ll also want to add the same further modifications to the STlist that spatialGE typically does. You might wonder – ifthose steps are not necessary for the normalization process, why are we doing them? We're going to do them because other functions fromspatialGEmay expect that information to be there. A strength of thespatialGE` package and its web application is that later functions expect quality control and normalization steps were performed. So something that the transformation function does, we’ll want to do so that later steps aren’t expecting it and can’t find it.

run_area_transformation <- function(stlist_obj, sample){
    
    # find median cell area
    median_area <- median(stlist_obj@spatial_meta[[sample]]$cell_area)
    # calculate cell specific size factors based on cell area
    size_factors <- stlist_obj@spatial_meta[[sample]]$cell_area / median_area
    # transform the counts using these size factors
    norm <- t(t(stlist_obj@counts[[sample]])/size_factors)
    # add a pseudocount of one to the transformed values so there are not zeroes and use a logarithm base of 2 
    stlist_obj@tr_counts[[sample]] <- log1p(norm) / log(2)

    # find gene avgs and stdevs and store
    stlist_obj@gene_meta[[sample]] <- tibble::tibble(gene_mean=as.vector(Matrix::rowMeans(stlist_obj@tr_counts[[sample]]))) %>%
      tibble::add_column(gene_stdevs=as.vector(apply(stlist_obj@tr_counts[[sample]], 1, sd))) %>%
      add_column(gene=rownames(stlist_obj@tr_counts[[sample]]), .before=1)

    return(stlist_obj)
}

for (sample_name in names(scz_spatial_tr@counts)){

}

We can visualize the library size for each cell within each sample.

combine_counts_annot <- function(matannot, matcount, sample_name, gene_name){
    full_join(
        matannot[[sample_name]][,c("libname", "annot")],
        matcount[[sample_name]][gene_name, ] %>% 
            data.frame() %>% 
            rownames_to_column("libname")
    ) %>% `colnames<-`(c("libname", "annot", sample_name))
}

use_combined_data <- function(mat, gene_name, use = "violin", samples = c("Br1139SCZ", "Br5314CTRL")){
  combined_data <- bind_rows(combine_counts_annot(mat@spatial_meta, mat@tr_counts, samples[1], gene_name),
                             combine_counts_annot(mat@spatial_meta, mat@tr_counts, samples[2], gene_name)) %>%
                      pivot_longer(starts_with("Br"),
                                   values_to = "tr_counts",
                                   names_to = "sample") %>%
                      drop_na()

  if (use == "violin"){
    return(
      combined_data %>%
        ggplot(aes(x = sample, 
               y = tr_counts, 
               fill = sample)) + 
        geom_violin() + 
        facet_wrap(~annot, scales = "free_y") + 
        theme_bw() + 
        scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.6) + 
        ggtitle(gene_name) +
        theme(legend.position = "bottom")
    )
  } else if (use == "summary"){
    table_length <- length(unique(combined_data$annot)) * 2
    return(
      combined_data %>%
        group_by(annot, sample) %>% 
        summarize(
              min_exp = min(tr_counts), 
              max_exp = max(tr_counts), 
              avg_exp = mean(tr_counts),
              median_exp = median(tr_counts),
              var_exp = var(tr_counts)
        ) %>% 
    print(n=table_length)
    )
  } else {
    message("No other downstream uses supported besides 'violin' and 'summary'")
  }
}

Glossary




Term
Definition


Barcodes
Cell identifiers. Typically IDs of random letters and numbers assigned to cells in single-cell or spatial experiments.


Centroid
The point corresponding to the geometric center of a shape. Has an x- and y- coordinate associated with it. Can be found if you know the vertices of a polygon.


Clustering
Grouping similar data points together into distinct sets based on shared qualities or data patterns. Specifically, the process of organizing unlabeled data points into groups such that data points in the same group are more similar to each other than to data points in other groups. Some way to compute distance or similarity is required for clustering methods.


Coefficient
Represents proportional relationship between variables. Within regression, quantifies how much the dependent variable changes when the independent variable changes by one unit.


Cohort
Research participants within the same study.


Color palette
Specific combination of colors used together within a visualization to represent data. May be a set of discrete colors from different color families or instead a range of different shades within a color family.


Compressed
A way to store data so that it requires less space. Due to the way that it is stored, it's less readable and often needs to be decompressed in order to visually inspect it or work with it.


Coordinates
A set of two numbers (x- and y-) used to represent a specific location on the two-dimensional Cartesian coordinate plane, specifically the x-axis communicates how far to move horizontally while the y-value communciates how far to move vertically from the origin of the plane (0,0). This can be visualized by drawing a vertical line from the x-coordinate on x-axis and a horizontal line from the y-coordinate on the y-axis and seeing where they intersect.


Counts
The quantitative measurement of RNA molecules detected for specific genes within a spatial location (e.g., spot or cell). May be detected by sequencing or fluorescent imaging within Spatial Transcriptomics experiments. Often represented in a matrix where rows represent counts for a specific gene and columns represent counts for a specific cell.


Deconvolution
A computational method used to estimate the types and proportions of individual cells present within a capture location that has a mixture of cells rather than representing a single-cell. Necessary for spatial technologies like Visium with their "spots", but generally can be used for any technology where there a mixture of cells is represented within the capture area.


Differential Gene Expression
The difference in expression of a gene between samples or cases. Differential expression is typically thought of as a difference in abundance or amount of expression but may also be a difference in what cell types a gene is expressed in or where a gene is expressed spatially within a tissue.


Directories
Folders in a file system.


Distribution
A mathematical description of the possible values of a random variable and how often each occurs.


Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex
dlPFC. An area of the prefrontal cortex in the frontal lobe of the brain. Situated towards the top and side of the prefrontal cortex. Involved in executive functioning and cognitive control, contributing to working memory, divergent thinking, executive attention, and decision making. Found to be central to cognitive dysfunction in schizophrenia.


Doublet
A cell segmentation boundary that contains signals or mRNA counts from two or more distinct cells rather than just one cell -- the result of an error in the image segmentation process.


Droplet
In single-cell sequencing, droplets are used to physically separate cells prior to sequencing.


Enrichment
Overrepresentation of something (e.g., a gene or set of genes) compared to expectation, other sets, or a background set.


Features
Used to describe the rows in a gene count matrix. Since genes correspond to the rows, the term features is often used interchangeably with "genes".


Filtering
The process of removing low quality or irrelevant data from a biological dataset. Often what will be filtered is identified during quality control.


Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded
FFPE. A biological sample is acquired through either surgial resection or biopsy and fixed with formalin to arrest cellular processes, crosslink proteins, and "fix" tissues. Then dehydration, clearing, and paraffin infiltration remove water and provide structural support to the sample before embedding the tissue in a paraffin block that can be sectioned or archived for long-term storage without ultra cold freezers. This method preserves tissue structure and morphological details though nucleic acids are often fragmented in the fixation process.


Fresh frozen
FF. Fresh frozen samples are biological tissue samples. Typically a sample is acquired through either surgical resection or biopsy and then rapidly frozen (without prior chemical fixation) using liquid nitrogen or dry ice to arrest cellular processes, and stored at ultra low temperatures until sectioning and further sample preparation steps can be performed. This method preserves cellular architecture and the quality nucleic acids for later analysis though overall morphological details may not be preserved. Additionally, any water inside the tissue will turn into ice crystals, distorting structure


GEO
Gene Expression Omnibus. A database storing high throughput gene expression datasets deposited by researchers.


GUI
Graphical User Interface. May be a web interface or a local application.


Guide
Another term for a legend in a plot.


Histology
The microscopic structure of a biological tissue, often visualized with a microscope and tissue staining to enhance contrast of structure.


Hypothesis generation
The process of formulating new ideas or testable answers for a research question by exploring data and other related knowledge or results within the field.


Image-based technologies
Methods that are used to directly visualize and map RNA transcripts using labeled fluorescent probes that bind directly to the transcripts within intact tissue sections. Automated cycles of high-resolution microscopy rather than sequencing methods are used to detect the hybridization of probes to the transcripts. These methods typically offer high cellular resolution but low molecular resolution only being able to be utilized for a limited panel of genes for each sample.


Index
To use a location/coordinate, name, or combination of coordinates or names to extract a specific value from a vector, matrix, or data frame.


laminar domains
Functional and structural anatomical subdivisions or layers which are distinct, spanning the brain tissue.


lapply
A function from base R that allows the user to loop through an input, performing a specified function on each input, returning the results in a list.


libname
IDs assigned to "libraries". Used interchangeably with "barcodes" by spatialGE.


log transformation
A data transformation typically used for raw counts data because it is heavily right-skewed due to data sparsity. A pseudocount of one is added to raw values and then a logarithm function is applied, resulting in a more bell-shaped normal distribution by pulling far away data closer to the rest of the data.


Loop
Automating a process by iterating over a set of inputs and executing the same code for each item in set (or until a stop condition is met).


Matrix
A two-dimensional or rectangular structure with horizontal rows and vertical columns that can be used to store related data (like cell-specific gene counts) in entries (where each row and column intersects).


Metadata
Descriptive information describing other data. Descriptions may include how or when that data was generated, source organisms, associated patient IDs, or demographic information.


Mitochondrial reads
Reads from a sequencing experiment that map to the mitochondrial genome of cells rather than the nuclear genome.


Morphology
The physical appearance within a biological sample like cells within a tissue. Histological images contain morphological information. Morphology images can represent the same tissue as a histological image, but they don't use the stains that histology does to visualize the tissue.


mRNA
Messenger RNA, a single-stranded nucleic acid which transfers genetic information. Transcribed from DNA, it will be translated into protein.


Multicellular
More than one cell is represented.


Neurotypical
A term used to describe donors / their brains based on neurological characterisics -- saying they align with the typical expectations for a population. Neurotypical refers to "control" in this case.


Package
A bundled collection of code or software designed to perform specific tasks. Users load these packages and consult their documentation in order to use functions for specific tasks.


Panel
A specific, curated set of molecular targets such as genes or transcripts.


Parquet
A file type that is used to efficiently store large amounts of data because it uses a column-by-column approach.


PCA
Principal component analysis. A dimensionality reduction method that finds principal components or orthogonal components that explain variation within the original dataset.


Personally Identifiable Information
Data unique to an individual person that can be used to distinguish their identity, including full names, Social Security numbers, contact information, etc.; abbreviated as "PII".


PMI
Postmortem Interval. The amount of time between the passing of a donor and when a tissue sample is taken from the donor. This interval of time is typically reported within hours but may be reported in another unit representing measurement of time. Shorten post mortem intervals correlate with higher tissue quality, minimizing the time for natural degradation to occur.


Polygon
A multi-sided two-dimensional shape. Each side is a straight line whose endpoints are each connected to an endpoint of another side. Circles or ovals can be approximated by a polygon with many sides.


Postmortem samples
Samples collected after the death of the donor.


Protected Health Information
A subset of PII that includes any health information that can identify an individual that is regulated by HIPAA, including full name, contact information, medical records, health insurance information, biometric elements, etc.; abbreviated as "PHI".


Pseudobulk
A data transformation where counts from single cells are aggregated and considered in bulk, typically by summing counts across all cells of the same cell type within a sample (though counts can be averaged alternatively). Pseudobulks mirror how the data would look if that specific cell population had been isolated and sequenced using a traditional bulk experiment.


Quality Control
The process of exploring and evaluating raw biological data to detect technical artifacts, errors, low quality data, biases, etc prior to downstream analysis in order to promote higher confidence results.


Quilt plot
A type of plot that is used to visualize the two-dimensional spatial distribution of gene expression or cell types/clusters within a sample, mirroring the physical architecture of the tissue sample. Colors are used to represent the expression values or cell type/domain classes. Can be thought of as a type of heatmap without any clustering.


R-squared
Statistical measure relating to the proportion of variability within the dependent varaible that can be explained by the independent variable and the relationship between the variables. Often used as a measure of effect size. Also known as the "coefficient of determination".


Random seed
A number provided as an initial starting value for random number generators, promoting the repeatability and reproducibility of random processes.


Repeatability
The ability for the same researcher to run the same analysis on the same data and get the same results.


Reproducible
A term used to describe research or a process that a new researcher can follow, running the same analysis on the same data and getting the same results as the original researcher..


Resolution
Refers to the smallest unit of change or observation scale that can reliably be detected or measured. High resolution means that a scale has fine intervals and small differences can be observed. Low resolution means that a scale has broader intervals and small variations may be missed (e.g., harder to differentiate between individual cells or measure all molecules).


RIN
RNA Integrity Number. A measure of sample quality determined by an automated software algorithm. Found by analyzing the electrophoretic separation of RNA molecules according to size, processing the resulting signal traces (electropherograms which representing how much of RNA of different sizes is present in samples) to evaluate and rank the signal features and combinations of features according to their predictive information content. Returns a value representing the overal level of RNA degradation within a sample on a standardized 1-10 scale.


Schizophrenia
Chronic neuropsychiatric disorder characterized by a spectrum of symptoms impacting a person's thoughts, emotions, and behavior. Symptoms are generally classified as positive, negative, or cognitive.


Segmentation
Process of inferring individual cell boundaries from tissue images, nuclear or other cell surface and interior marker staining, and transcript coordinates. Some algorithms if only provided nuclear staining first segment nuclear boundaries and expand them to approximate the cell boundaries. Others use the combination of stains to first find cell boundaries. After inferring cell boundaries, observed transcripts can be assigned to cells.


Sequencing
A laboratory technique that extracts and analyzes the genetic material from a sample.


Sequencing-based technologies
Methods that utilize microscopic regions or spots on specialized slides to sequence intact tissues, retaining the original physical location of observed RNA molecules within a tissue sample. These methods have high molecular resolution but low cellular resolution because they sequence the whole transcriptome rather than targeting a limited set of genes. However, the spots are not necessarily single-cells and data must be deconvoluted.


Slope
Coefficient within a linear model that represents both the steepness and direction of the relationship between the independent and dependent variable.


Sparse
Term used to describe the results from a single-cell or spatial transcriptomics experiment. Typically means that an experiment is low coverage, possibly because a given cell has a limited number of molecules that are being expressed at any given time. Within a data matrix, this looks like a lot of zeros. A sparse-matrix representation, on the other hand, omits these zeros, storing only the location of and values of non-zero data (though displays of this data may include periods instead of zeros if inspected). This sparse representation is used to reduce the overall storage size needed for the data.


Spatial Transcriptomics
Spatial Transcriptomics refers to molecular methods used to measure gene expression at or near single-cell resolution, reporting where observed transcripts are physically located within the source tissue, preserving spatial context.


Specialized cell
A highly differentiated cell that serves a specific purpose within a tissue. It may have a unique structure (physical shape or size) compared to other cells. It will express specific genes that other cells may not.


Spot
Refers to the regions across a tissue section that sequencing-based methods use to capture spatially-resolved data. Spots often represent 10s to 100s of cells (e.g., multicellular) rather than single-cells. Each spot has a defined set of x- and y- coordinates on the slide used to capture data, relating captured data to physical locations within the tissue.


STlist
An S4 object that the spatialGE program uses to store spatially-resolved expression data for one or multiple samples. Utilizes slots for various aspects of the data and named lists within each slot to store data specific to each sample.


Subcellular
Represents part of a cell rather than a whole, single cell.


Transcriptome
Complete collection of transcripts produced by the genome in a specific cell, tissue, or organism.


Vertex
Where the endpoints of two edges meet in a polygon.


Violin plot
A plot used to visualize distributions of numerical variables. Because they visualize the density of data across possible values of the variable, they may resemble violins. Useful for comparing the variable across different biological groups.


Visium
A popular sequencing-based technology for generating spatially-resolved expression data.


Volcano plot
A scatter plot that plots data points according to the observed magnitude of change on the x-axis and the statistical significance on the y-axis. Typically one point represents one gene, and the values are found by comparing the expression of that gene across different experimental conditions or clinical cases. Points are often colored differently based on whether the gene is upregulated (over-expressed) or downregulated (under-expressed) in a specific case relative to a conrol and whether the observed change reached pre-defined thresholds for statistical significance.


Xenium
A popular image-based technology for geenrating spatially-resolved expression data.
